newsitem.title: RWANDA: Weary refugees scavenge for food in Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: Weary refugees scavenge for food in Rwanda.

text.p: Rwandan soldiers prevented returning Hutu refugees from gaining access to a U.N. transit centre for the second day on Tuesday, leaving thousands of refugees to scavenge in the countryside for food.

Two Rwandan soldiers stood guard outside the gate of the largely empty centre at Nkamira, 21 km (13 miles) northeast of the border town of Gisenyi, stopping the refugees from entering to rest, sleep and get food as planned by the U.N. refugee agency.

Thousands of refugees who had joined the mass exodus from Zaire blocked the main street of Nkamira. There was near chaos as they fought to board buses and trucks towards their home villages which they had fled in 1994.
Thousands more had given up fighting for places and were camped on the roadside on the town's northern outskirts, sheltering under tarpaulin or scavenging in the surrounding countryside for food.
Some said they had run out of food completely after camping there for three days.
They said the authorities wanted them to keep walking to the next transit centre at Ruhengeri, 65 km (40 miles) northeast of Gisyeni where they crossed into Rwanda from Zaire.
But they said they had no more energy to walk and would remain there until they were fed.
Aid agencies attempted to distribute biscuits to the tide of refugees over the weekend but abandoned the exercise when it sparked riots.
Aid workers said a line of people, with breaks here and there of a few hundred metres, stretched all the way from the border to Ruhengeri.
UNHCR had said it would bring in 100 buses from Uganda on Monday to ease the problem, but they were delayed by bureaucratic hurdles between Ugandan and Rwandan authorities.
The Hutus fled Rwanda in 1994 after a Tutsi-led army overran the country following the genocide of up to a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus by Hutu extremists.
The few people who have made it back to their villages said there had been no animosity from their former Tutsi neighbours.

Lambert Dushiminana, a 25-year-old former law student, said he arrived back in Rubavu, 12 km (8 miles) northeast of Gisenyi, on Sunday evening with his wife and brother after walking two days from Mugunga camp.
"No one has made any accusations against the returnees since they arrived here and I regret not coming back earlier," he said.
Phinias Musemakweli, 43, returned to his home in a poor district in the outskirts of Ruhengeri with his wife and three daughters on Sunday.
"All the people welcomed us. We're happy because we have returned home at last. We have no fear for our security, the reason why we left Zaire was we were too frightened," he said.
Asked whether he trusted the Rwandan government to protect him, he said: "I trust them a little, I'm waiting to see."
His eldest daughter was asked whether Tutsis in the same district had said anything to them. "They saw us but have said nothing to us since we arrived," she replied.
"They are our brothers and welcomed us back," her father added quickly.
